entities.name: Benjamin Wade
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Benjamin Franklin 'Bluff' Wade (1800–1878) was an Ohio Radical Republican US Senator (1851–1869) who came within a single Senate vote of becoming President of the United States — the man who would have succeeded Andrew Johnson had the 1868 impeachment conviction succeeded. As Senate president pro tempore during the trial, Wade was next in the presidential line of succession, having helped organize the very impeachment that would have elevated him to the presidency — a constitutional conflict of interest that may have contributed to his vote-counting difficulties.

Wade was one of the most militant and uncompromising Radical Republicans in Congress — a fierce anti-slavery advocate who had delivered one of the most provocative abolitionist speeches in Senate history in the 1850s, and who co-authored the Wade-Davis Bill (1864) with Henry Winter Davis — the most stringent congressional Reconstruction plan, which Lincoln pocket-vetoed. The Wade-Davis Manifesto that followed was one of the sharpest public attacks on a president by members of his own party in American history.

Known as 'Bluff' Wade for his blunt, combative style — he routinely responded to death threats by saying he would meet any challenger in the street — Wade was one of the most personally fearless politicians of the era. He came from abolitionist northeastern Ohio and had practiced law while actively helping escaped slaves.

His defeat for re-election in 1869 — after Johnson's acquittal and the Republican machine's consolidation around Grant — ended a career that had come extraordinarily close to the presidency.
